newsitem.title: USA: Congress urged not to jeopardize tobacco suits.
newsitem.headline: Congress urged not to jeopardize tobacco suits.

text.p: Iowa Attorney General Thomas Miller urged Congress on Thursday not to pass any bills that would prevent states from suing tobacco companies for reimbursement of tobacco-related health costs.
Miller made the plea at a House Judiciary Committee hearing on legislation to limit damages in product liability suits. Iowa is one of 22 states suing the tobacco companies.

"Any asserted tort reform legislation that would limit the ability of victims of tobacco products to obtain civil justice, or that would prevent states from seeking reimbursement for health-related tobacco costs, should be opposed," Miller said.

"According to the recent Liggett admissions, the tobacco industry has known for years about the health risks and the addictive qualities of its products," Miller added. "The victims of this deception should be allowed to seek fair compensation."
Liggett made the admissions last month as part of a settlement of the suit by the states.

The committee was considering legislation that would limit punitive damages in product liability cases to twice the actual damages, or $250,000, whichever is greater. Similar bills were pending in the Senate.

President Bill Clinton vetoed a product liability bill last year, but Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, said he was confident Congress would pass a new bill that Clinton would sign.
"As poll after poll shows, the American public wants reform of our current out-of-control legal system. And they deserve it," Hyde said.

He said the committee would try to write a bill that would fairly balance the interests of both plaintiffs and defendants in product liability cases. The bill is backed by business groups such as the National Association of Manufacturers.
"I am confident that this committee and this Congress wil once again produce a bipartisan package of reforms, and one which the president will sign into law," Hyde said.
Hyde said imposing limits on punitive damages for negligence or misconduct, which are often several times the amount of actual damages, would encourage settlements and discourage frivolous lawsuits.

But Miller said punitive damages were a major deterrent to corporate wrongdoing and should not be capped. "Given the billions of profits reaped by the tobacco industry, a punitive damages award limited by statute is unlikely to have that effect," he said.
